newsitem.title: USA: Minnesota official sees low odds for Twins stadium.
newsitem.headline: Minnesota official sees low odds for Twins stadium.

text.p: The Minnesota Twins, an American League baseball club that wants a new stadium, might be in for a disappointment when it comes to getting state residents to help foot the bill, the Minnesota treasurer said on Tuesday.

"There is just no sentiment in the state, none, for using public dollars, when you have a billionaire, who is the owner...It won't be bonded, definitely," Michael McGrath, the state treasurer, told Reuters in an interview.
McGrath, who was in Boston for a National Association of State Auditors, Comptrollers and Treasurers conference, was referring to Twins owner Carl Pohlad.

Gov. Arne Carlson has proposed a plan that would give the state a 49 percent ownership stake in the team and keep title to a new, $350 million to $400 million retractable roof stadium. But even if state lawmakers approve the project, McGrath said it still would face an uphill battle.
"There's no chance taxpayers will not rebel, if for some reason, the legislature does approve it, and it's possible, things happen."

The state official stressed that Minnesotans do not want to lose the popular baseball team, which has threatened to pull up stakes, but speculated that if the state were to back a new stadium, other professional sports teams, including the National Football League Vikings and National Basketball Association Timberwolves, might make the same sorts of requests.
"To me, it's 50-50 as to whether the Twins will be there in the 1999 season," he added, noting the team wants a decision by the end of this year.
Minnesota survived losing the North Stars National Hockey League franchise to Dallas. Minneapolis-St. Paul in June was selected as one for four cities for a new NHL franchise.
Carlson is expected to call a special session in September to consider financing for a Twins stadium.
